title: Kamma in the moment
hookLine: the "impulsion" moments where intention does its work

lines: LOOK, PICK IT UP, TEST IT.
cards: A man is asleep under a mango tree with his head covered. A ripe mango drops and brushes past his ear. He wakes, uncovers his head, and looks.
He reaches out and picks the fruit up. He squeezes it, sniffs it, decides it's good. Then he eats it.
The commentaries tell that simile, and every step in it stands for one stage of a single act of perception. The falling fruit, the turning, the looking, the testing. But only one step is the eating.

teach.b: When something strikes a sense door, the Abhidhamma says, the mind runs a set series of moments. It turns toward the object. It sees, or hears.
It receives, investigates and settles what the thing is. None of that is kamma yet. It's the man waking, looking, testing.
Then come the moments the manual calls javana, usually translated impulsion, or running. In an ordinary sense process they usually run seven times in a row.
This is the eating: where the mind doesn't only know the mango but takes it, likes it, wants it, pushes it away, or meets it with kindness. And this is where the manual locates kamma.

Back on day three hundred seventy-two, you met the Buddha's plain words: intention is what I call kamma; having intended, a person acts by body, speech and mind. The Abhidhamma gives that sentence an address.
Kamma isn't stored in some far-off ledger. It's made in these few running moments, wholesome or unwholesome, again and again, all day. So javana is where a life changes direction.
You can't stop the mango from falling. You can't unsee it.

But a pause, a breath, a moment of knowing what you're about to do, and the next run of javana can go a different way. After matter, a living body and the speed of it all, this is where the speed turns into a choice.

how: In Theravada Abhidhamma study, students learn the series of mind-moments in a sense process, often through the commentaries' mango simile, and teachers point to the javana moments as the place where kamma is made.

o: the merit that comes back from a good deed
the running moments where intention makes kamma
the first moment the mind turns to an object

games.q: the mango simile: tap the pairs.
p: the object strikes a sense door

s: in the Abhidhamma, simply seeing something makes kamma
seeing, receiving and settling are not kamma; kamma is made in the javana moments that follow.
the Buddha said intention is what he calls kamma
having intended, a person acts by body, speech and mind.
in an ordinary sense process, javana usually runs seven times
so the manual says: seven running moments, wholesome or unwholesome.

games.q: you're the man under the mango tree. the fruit has fallen, you've looked at it and tested it. in the simile, which step stands for javana?
games.why: the eating. the waking, looking and testing stand for the stages before; the eating is javana, the moments that take the object.

practice: Sit still and wait for an impulse: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, open your eyes, check the time. When it comes, don't follow it right away; name it quietly, wanting to move, and feel what happens in the pause.
Then, if you choose to, move, knowing that you're moving.

wordCard.voice: Javana. Impulsion, the running moments after the mind knows its object, where intention does its work and kamma is made. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: impulsion, running; the moments in a sense process where intention does its work.

carryVoice: Your line: where kamma is made. The mango falls either way; the taking is where a life turns. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.63 (Nibbedhika Sutta), intention is kamma
